title: Make the backup transport send bytes, with a real socket test
value: Turn one foundational networking stub into a working, verifiable transport primitive. A reliable send-all function is reusable by both file transfers and protocol headers, and gives the backup project an honest first end-to-end byte-transfer demonstration.
why_now: This review expanded beyond the previous candidates and found a stronger, tightly scoped opportunity. At backup-project revision adf40a00b1c806972c8dbd28acc7284f3ba19749, network.h promises that network_send_all sends every byte, but network.c ignores all its arguments and returns success. The existing network test only checks receive-buffer initialization, so it does not verify the send contract. These are explicitly marked implementation stubs, not an undisclosed production regression. Implementing and testing this single primitive has more immediate functional value than another presentation improvement and is smaller than completing the whole backup service. The earlier channel runner is still useful and unimplemented in its unchanged inspected revision, but a no-op transport that reports success now takes priority. Source and test files were reviewed; no C or scheduler tests were executed in this planning review.
effort: About 2-3 hours on Linux or WSL, including focused socket tests
steps: Implement only network_send_all against its existing header contract: advance through short writes, retry interrupted sends, and return an error on actual failure or a zero-progress send instead of looping forever or reporting success.

Define and document edge cases for zero-length input and invalid arguments. Choose a platform-appropriate SIGPIPE policy so sending to a disconnected peer returns an error instead of unexpectedly terminating the process; retain the project's stated Linux/macOS portability where supported.

Extend test_network with an actual socketpair transfer and an independent receiver, comparing an exact binary payload including zero bytes. Drain large payloads concurrently so the test cannot deadlock on socket-buffer capacity.

Add focused short-write and EINTR coverage through a controlled test seam or equivalent deterministic technique, plus disconnected-peer and zero-length cases. Run the existing make test and CI workflow and document that other networking functions remain stubs.
acceptance_checks: A local socketpair receiver obtains the exact payload and byte count for both a small binary buffer and a payload larger than normal socket-buffer capacity.
Deterministic short writes and interrupted calls complete correctly without dropped or duplicated bytes; zero-progress and permanent errors terminate with the documented error result.
A disconnected peer does not produce a false success or unexpected SIGPIPE process termination, and the zero-length case behaves as documented.
Existing project tests still pass, the new transport tests actually exercise network_send_all, and documentation does not claim the remaining listener, receive, or connection stubs are complete.

evidence.observation: The network_send_all contract explicitly requires looping around send until all bytes are transferred, returning zero on success and minus one on error.
The inspected network_send_all is marked as a stub, casts sockfd, data, and count to void, and unconditionally returns zero. Other networking functions are also marked as stubs.
The current test initializes recv_buf_t and asserts that len and start are zero. It does not create sockets or call network_send_all.
The existing Ubuntu CI installs build dependencies and runs make all and make test, providing an existing place for a real transport regression test.
Fresh inspection confirms the solver still converts W and unpacks W.shape without explicit channel-matrix validation. The previously proposed custom-channel runner remains a worthwhile alternative.

The inspected main function hardcodes Processes.txt, runs the simulation, prints metrics, and unconditionally calls generate_gantt_chart; it exposes no command-line input or no-plot option in this entry point.
The README describes a file-driven scheduler with waiting and turnaround metrics, logs, and a Matplotlib window, making repeatable headless execution a plausible usability improvement.

alternatives.title: Build the previously proposed validated custom-channel runner
alternatives.reason_not_selected: Still useful and supported by the unchanged source and README. However, replacing a backup transport no-op with an actual byte-transfer primitive provides a more foundational functional gain at a similar or smaller estimated effort. The earlier proposal is not marked completed.

alternatives.title: Add configurable input and a headless metrics mode
alternatives.reason_not_selected: The hardcoded input path and unconditional plotting in main make this a credible usability task. A reliable metrics-output contract needs more examination of scheduler behavior and expected results; the backup send contract and missing test are already precise.
